Welcome to the VideoMonitor page. In short, VideoMonitor is a graphical shell for FFmpeg that we tried to make convenient, stable, and still flexible for everyday work. Instead of keeping and retyping long command lines, you get an interface that stores your FFmpeg commands as presets, sits in the tray, and does a lot of the routine for you. A few of the extra pieces: yt-dlp integration for downloads from the network (we call these miners). Step-by-step FFmpeg processing so effects can be chained (denoise, then stabilize). A schedule so heavy encodes can wait for night or the weekend. CPU limits, including a cap on how many cores encoding may use, so a background encode does not take the machine away from other work. Separate output directories – the job can be repeated safely, and the originals stay untouched. Notifications by Telegram or email when a job finishes or fails. Note: The program is in a public beta for now.

Runners – the FFmpeg shell, and the presets that ship with it. Miners – the yt-dlp shell, and how a miner can hand files to a runner. Usage scenarios – real ways to use VideoMonitor. The options live on the Settings tab. They are stored in VideoMonitor.toml next to the program. You can edit that file yourself; it is loaded at startup, and a later edit in the interface writes the file again. If you found a bug or have an idea, please post it on GitHub (VideoMonitorDocs). For playback, we recommend MPC-HC (Media Player Classic). It handles subtitles and chapters (like on YouTube), you can shape it to the way you watch, and it feels right (on the GitHub page see Releases). Download the app | Privacy | License

VideoMonitor is a program for everyday video work. It runs FFmpeg for you and can download video with yt-dlp, so the commands do not have to be typed again each time. The program is written in Rust. The window is drawn with Iced, a Rust library. Iced belongs to the Iced project. Encoding is done by FFmpeg. You install FFmpeg yourself. FFmpeg belongs to the FFmpeg project. Downloads are done by yt-dlp. You install yt-dlp yourself. yt-dlp belongs to the yt-dlp project. Copyright (c) Vladimir Zubkov. All rights reserved.

A miner downloads video through yt-dlp. The source field is either an http / https link or a directory. Browse picks a directory, not a single file. A path to one file in that field is not walked by Drill. Link files live inside a directory. The miner walks the tree and picks up .url, .webloc, .desktop shortcuts, .m3u / .m3u8 playlists, and text files that match the mask (out of the box *.url). You can drop a shortcut onto the row: the source becomes the URL itself. Drop a file of links or a playlist, and the source becomes its parent directory. Where downloads go: if the destination directory is empty, the video lands next to the address file. You can set another directory — everything goes there. For a source tree there is a Preserve dir structure when downloading checkbox: the layout of directories with shortcuts is then mirrored under the destination. A URL source has no such checkbox: there is no tree. Drill builds a queue and starts the download. yt-dlp options go in the row. Under that is a preset bank: a click fills in a ready-made option. To save your own text into a slot, hold Ctrl and click the preset. The Miners tab: source, yt-dlp options, destination, and Drill.

After Drill the program goes through: collect the list → check the queue → download Collect the list: a local directory is walked, skipping system folders (.git, node_modules, and the like). Links come from shortcuts, playlists, .vmtxt files, and PL... file names. Each link is one queue job. Check the queue: for each row yt-dlp asks for the full description (-J): title, duration, video and audio formats, subtitles for the table. The miner row often shows progress such as "checking source: 3 of 12". Download: a normal yt-dlp run down the queue. Progress is on the miner row or on the Performance tab. While the queue check is running, the row shows Download now and Stop. Download now starts downloading from what is already known, without waiting for the rest of the check. Pause applies once yt-dlp is already downloading a file: the process is held. Resume continues the check or the download.

The table shows Video and Audio chips for the resolutions and audio bitrates that are available. Formats shared by every video in the list are bold. Click a chip to put that format into the yt-dlp options line. Subtitles: open the section and pick languages. The app folds them into one --sub-langs argument. Columns can be sorted. The table is also moved with the keyboard (arrows or Tab).

Like runners, miners can run one at a time. The reason is different: not to take the whole network link, while runners are kept from taking the whole CPU. Miners started later wait with the status Queued.

A miner can be linked to a runner: on the miner row you pick the runner's letter. When the download finishes, the linked runner picks up the downloaded files, if that is allowed in Settings → Coordination. Several miners can be linked to one runner, and that runner encodes the downloads one after another.
If the yt-dlp options would download video with no audio, or audio with no video, the program warns you. It can add the missing stream so you get a full file, or you can continue as written.
Action Keys Start (Drill) D (when F2 is on) or the Drill button Focus the download queue Ctrl+Space (on the Miners tab) Browse the source Ctrl+Enter Browse the destination Ctrl+Alt+Enter

Miner presets are a shared bank of yt-dlp format strings. A click loads the slot into the selected miner. The program ships six presets. There is no separate 360p slot. Reset miner presets puts this set back. Miners do not chain presets. A chain of up to five is a runner feature.

Preset Format string Up to 2160p (4K – large file) bestvideo[height<=2160]+bestaudio, then 1440, 1080, then best Up to 1080p bestvideo[height<=1080]+bestaudio, then 720, 480, then best Up to 720p bestvideo[height<=720]+bestaudio, then 480, 360, then best Up to 480p bestvideo[height<=480]+bestaudio, then 360, then best Audio only (best available) bestaudio/best Best progressive (single file ≤1080p) best[height<=1080]/best – one file, no separate video and audio merge

A runner is one FFmpeg job. You say where the files are, how to process them, and where to put the result. On the Runners tab each row has an options field and a preset bank. A click on a preset fills in a ready-made FFmpeg command. You can type your own command in the same field. To save it, hold Ctrl and click the preset. The program checks whether the command is valid, and if it is fine — writes it into the chosen preset. FFmpeg and ffprobe must be on the system PATH. Without them a runner will not start. Whether FFmpeg is installed, where it came from, and which version it is, shows under the header of the runners window. VideoMonitor can install FFmpeg from inside the program: open the Settings tab; in the Libraries block at the bottom of the window, next to the message that FFmpeg is not installed, there will be an Install button. For the install we recommend a package manager, for example Scoop. It helps you install and update the tools you need, including FFmpeg, and it takes care of the system PATH: checking, adding, and removing entries.

Open Runners and pick a row, for example A. Set the directory with the source files and a mask of files to process, for example *.mp4. Filename fragments work too; you can write several conditions separated by commas or spaces. Pick a preset or type the FFmpeg options. Set where the finished files should go. Press Start. The status column at the bottom shows what the runner is doing right now: watching the directory, encoding, waiting in the queue, or paused. Whatever you change on screen, the program writes into VideoMonitor.toml next to itself. You can edit this file by hand: the program picks up the new settings at once, or on the next launch if it is not running. The Runners tab: the table, the selected row, and the presets.

documents.t: In sequential mode only one runner runs. The others wait in the order they were started. Parallel mode lets several runners work at once. Load can be limited by each runner's priority or by the CPU cap, so the computer stays usable. The simplest cap is a count of cores. A percent cap is also there, but it is only a rough limit, because the process cannot be controlled completely.

Output files get comment tags that start with VM@. In the handmade file table those rows look faded and carry an @. The comment also stores the FFmpeg compression options that were used. Files VideoMonitor has already processed carry this @VM metadata tag in the description, so they are not processed again even if they land back in the originals folder. To work on individual files, open their list. It appears when you pick files with Select files… to the right of the mask, or with Show queue after the runner has scanned the directory, next to the originals path. There you can clear the VM@ mark, or mark files that have not been processed yet so the runner skips them. Right-click a media row and choose mark as processed, clear the processed mark, or remove from the list. An orange tint means the file already has a result whose options do not match the current FFmpeg arguments, so it may be encoded again (that depends on the settings).

If encoding should run on weekends or at night, set a schedule. Outside the allowed hours the runner shows as Scheduled in orange and waits. FFmpeg does not start. An encode that is already running may pause, depending on the "outside the window" setting. The windows are in Settings → App behavior → Deferred actions. They apply to runners first, and the same conditions can be put on miners. They are program-wide. Separate schedules for runners and miners, or a schedule per row, are not available, and a per-row schedule is probably not worth building.

This is not on screen until you ask for it. On the Runners tab, hold Ctrl+Space. Start becomes Playlist on every row. A click writes a playlist for the directory and its subdirectories from that runner's settings. The playlist format is chosen in Settings, for example M3U8. FFmpeg does not encode while the playlist is written.

Action Keys Start the selected runner G (when F2 is on) or the Start button Browse the source Ctrl+Enter Add files Ctrl+Shift+Enter Browse the destination Ctrl+Alt+Enter Focus the manual queue Ctrl+Shift+Space Show playlist buttons Hold Ctrl+Space Move a list row Ctrl+↑/↓ (runner list and the manual queue)

Runner presets are a shared bank of FFmpeg commands. A click loads the slot into the selected runner. The bank itself changes when you save, or when auto-save is on. The program ships 14 presets. Reset runner presets puts this set back. Double-click an existing slot to edit it in the preset wizard. The wizard builds the FFmpeg options for a slot: codec, container, quality, audio, and filters, including combinations (letterbox with edge blur, stabilize, denoise, loudness). Auto picks how hard to compress each file from its quality and from the minimum and maximum compression bounds you set (this is a VideoMonitor option, not an FFmpeg one). Heavy filters are split across the Options tabs. The + slot is a new preset, and that is when the wizard suggests a name. Ctrl+Shift+click builds a chain of up to five presets. Each preset runs its own tabs first, then the next preset. One preset holds up to three option tabs.

Preset What it does H.264 balanced H.264, medium preset, CRF 23, AAC 128k. A steady size and quality. H.265 compact (auto) Per file. Video CRF moves between 24 and 32. Audio bitrate moves between 320k and 128k. The markers are @v:middle and @a:high. H.265 720p compact (resize) Scales to 1280 wide, H.265 CRF 26, AAC 128k. AV1 compact SVT-AV1, preset 6, CRF 32, AAC 128k. Keeps the source size. Denoise (highpass+afftdn) High-pass and FFT denoise. Video is copied. Chain Loudness next. Loudness (loudnorm) Loudness to −16 LUFS. Video is copied. Use after Denoise. Stabilize Two tabs: detect shake, then transform and unsharp. Cut freeze+silence (copy) Finds frozen picture that is also silent and cuts those stretches with stream copy. Letterbox H→V (1080×1920) Horizontal frame on a vertical canvas. The side bars are a blur of the same picture. Letterbox V→H (1920×1080) Vertical frame on a horizontal canvas, same blur. Audio only (AAC) Drops the picture and writes AAC 192k. Remux copy (fix TS) Stream copy. Error flags are applied at the end of the command, just before the output file. Screen record (1080p cap) Records the desktop, capped at 1080p, no system audio. Start adds the output file. Stream (RTMP) Same capture, sent as FLV. Start adds the runner stream URL. FFmpeg does not host viewers.
VideoMonitor is flexible, but you do not have to build complex commands from scratch. Here are a few common ways to use the program right out of the box.

If you have a folder full of heavy video files from a camera or phone, you can shrink them to save space. Go to the Runners tab. Put the folder with your videos in the Source field. Choose a preset like H.265 compact from the preset bank on the right. Pick an Output folder so your original files stay safe. Press Start. The runner will go through the files one by one and save the compressed versions.

You can download an entire YouTube playlist or check a channel for new videos. Go to the Miners tab. Paste the URL of the playlist or channel into the Source field. Pick a preset like Up to 1080p or Audio only. Set an Output folder. Press Drill. If you tick the Monitor checkbox, the miner will remember what it already downloaded. Next time you press Drill, it will only fetch the new videos.
documents.s: 2. Downloading a playlist or a channel

documents.t: You can tell a runner to wait for a miner and process the files as soon as they finish downloading. This is great for downloading podcasts and converting them to a specific format. Set up a Miner to download your videos. Set up a Runner (for example, Runner A) with the Audio only (AAC) preset. On the miner row, find the linking dropdown and select Runner A. Press Drill on the miner. When the miner finishes downloading a file, Runner A will automatically pick it up and extract the audio.

Encoding takes a lot of CPU power. If you need to use your computer during the day, you can tell VideoMonitor to work only at night. Press F2 to turn on shortcuts, then press T to open the schedule. Select the hours when the program is allowed to work (for example, 01:00 to 07:00). Start your runners. They will wait quietly and show as Scheduled. When the allowed time comes, they will wake up, do the work, and pause again if the time runs out.

You can record your desktop directly from the program without setting up OBS. Go to the Runners tab. Pick the Screen record (1080p cap) preset. Press Start. The runner will record your screen and save it to the output folder. Press Stop when you are done.

VideoMonitor runs on your computer. This is what the beta sends out. Your settings, presets, and folders stay in VideoMonitor.toml next to the program. The log stays there too, if you turned logging on. After you accept the license, the program keeps an install id locally and only sends a hash of it. If the last run crashed, a short note stays until you send a report or dismiss it. Support the project (donate) opens Stripe. Stripe takes the card details. After you accept the license, the program can send a small note to the license service: the hashed install id, the version, the operating system, and what kind of note it is (a daily check-in, a finished runner or miner, a crash, or space saved). A finished job can include how many seconds of media it was, and how many bytes were saved. The daily check-in can include a few on/off settings, such as adaptive load, the schedule, and whether mail or Telegram is on. Folder paths, file names, mail, tokens, cookies, and preset text are not included. The same service tells the program whether the beta is still on, whether donations and sales are on, and a minimum version. Bugs and ideas opens a public GitHub issue. Whatever you write there is public. GitHub also counts how many times each release file is downloaded. Those counts are copied across when a new release replaces the old one. Send crash report is a separate note you choose to send. You can include a shortened log. Dismiss sends nothing.
